newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan lowers 1996/97 coffee production forecast.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan lowers 1996/97 coffee production forecast.

text.p: Kenyan coffee authorities have again revised forecasts for 1996/97 production downwards, citing weather and disease as major farm problems.
Senior Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) officials projected 1996/97 (October/September) output at 85,000 tonnes, down from earlier forecasts of 100,000, 95,000 and lately 90,000.
Flavian Mwangi, chairman of the Mild Coffee Traders Association (MCTA), saw an 11 percent decline in production in 1996/97 from a figure of 96,000 tonnes in 1995/96.
"This decline is caused by an insurgence of coffee berry disease in the main growing areas around Mount Kenya," Mwangi said in his MCTA chairman's annual report.
Mwangi said the top grade-growing cooperative (smallholder) sector was likely to be affected more due to lack of adequate fungicide sprays against the disease.

"Whereas the cooperatives have continued to lose their market share in the national coffee production, lately from 65 percent to 55 percent, estates coffee production has increased from 35 percent to 45 percent of national production," he said.
Smallholders have persistently complained that they have no access to credit facilities or cash to purchase farm inputs.
A senior official at the Coffee Board said the extent of damage from coffee berry disease was not yet known. The disease has affected main growing areas of central province.
"To say, like Mr Mwangi, that production is down mainly on the coffee disease is not entirely accurate. There are other things, such as weather, that affect production," he said.
"Our current revised forecast is based on these things; that forecast could be revised again depending on how these factors change," the official told Reuters in Nairobi.
Other coffee players cited the production cycle as one reason for a decline. They said that the trees produced more or less depending on the cycle, and this year was one of decline.
On scarcity of coffee at Kenya's weekly export auctions, a senior coffee board official said the board had sold most of what it was given by millers throughout the year.
"Sales are usually low in December. But the main issue is that we have already sold most of what we had," he said.

"With a liberalised market, farmers have stopped withholding their coffees because they realise that if global prices go down they will make losses -- they have no government support mechanism for domestic prices," he added.

The auction on December 3 was cancelled due to scarcity of coffee and prices rose at the next auctions on December 10 and 17 on tight supply. The market has now closed for Christmas and New Year holidays and will reopen on January 7 when the board will offer only 18,000 60-kg bags of coffee for sale. --Nairobi Newsroom ++254-2 330-261.
